source.quote: attack, in relation to the behaviour of a dog, does not include behaviour which was an immediate response to, and was induced by, provocation, but includes (a)...(d)..., unless the owner establishes that the behaviour was justified by a reasonable cause

readings.description: The provocation exclusion (an immediate response induced by provocation is not an 'attack' at all) is a separate, categorical carve-out. The trailing 'unless the owner establishes... reasonable cause' qualifies only the (a)-(d) inclusion list that follows it: conduct within (a)-(d) counts as an attack unless the owner shows it was reasonably justified, but conduct that was a provoked immediate response never becomes an attack regardless of reasonableness.

citations.cite: Dog Act 1976 (WA) s. 3 'attack' — the exclusion clause is set off by its own 'but includes' before the (a)-(d) list begins

readings.description: 'Unless the owner establishes... reasonable cause' qualifies the entire definition, including the provocation exclusion, so even a provoked immediate response could still count as an attack if the owner cannot show reasonable cause.
readings.rejection_rationale: This reading would make the provocation exclusion almost entirely dependent on the same reasonable-cause proviso as the inclusion list, collapsing a clause the drafter set apart with its own 'but includes' into the list it introduces, and it would require the dog's owner to justify behaviour the definition has already said is not an attack.

taken.rationale: The categorical reading gives the 'but includes' clause independent work to do and does not require an owner to justify conduct the exclusion has already placed outside the definition.

site.anchor: `the dog counted as a dangerous dog for a s 33D penalty`

source.quote: for an offence relating to a dangerous dog, a fine of $20 000, but the minimum penalty is a fine of $1 000; ... for an offence relating to a dog other than a dangerous dog, a fine of $10 000

readings.description: Whether an offence 'relates to a dangerous dog' for s. 33D penalty purposes is assessed by the dog's dangerous-dog status AT THE TIME OF THE ATTACK. A s. 33E declaration made only after that attack — including one founded on that very attack under s. 33E(1)(a) — does not retroactively engage the dangerous-dog penalty band for that offence, because s. 33F(3) fixes the declaration's own effect at 7 days after notice, before which the dog was not yet 'a dangerous dog (declared)'. (A dog that is independently a dangerous dog (restricted breed) or commercial security dog by breed or function is, of course, already within the dangerous-dog band at the time of any attack, with no declaration needed.)

citations.cite: Dog Act 1976 (WA) s. 33F(3) — the declaration 'has effect 7 days after the giving of a notice'
Dog Act 1976 (WA) s. 33E(1)(a) — a declaration may itself be founded on the same attack

readings.description: The dog's dangerous-dog status is assessed as at prosecution or sentencing for the s. 33D offence, so a dog later declared dangerous (even because of the very attack being prosecuted) attracts the higher penalty band for that same attack.
readings.rejection_rationale: This reading lets a later declaration retroactively aggravate the penalty for an already-completed offence, on facts the offender could not have known applied to them at the time of the conduct being punished — an unusual result for a penal provision, and one the statute's use of a prospective 7-day effective date for declarations (s. 33F(3)) does nothing to support.

taken.rationale: Assessing a penal status element as at the time of the conduct, not as at trial, is the ordinary criminal-law default, and nothing in ss 33D/33E/33F displaces it; s. 33F(3)'s own prospective effective date for a declaration positively supports it.

witnesses: `the s 33D(1) penalty band` — a dog with no prior dangerous-dog status that attacks and is declared dangerous under s 33E(1)(a) *because of that attack*: statusAtTimeOfOffence yields the non-dangerous-dog band ($10 000) for that attack; statusAtTimeOfProsecution would yield the dangerous-dog band ($20 000 / $1 000 minimum).

entries.delegated_field: RevocationApplication's `the local government is satisfied the dog can be kept without the likelihood of any contravention of this Act`

source.quote: if the local government is satisfied that the dog can be kept without the likelihood of any contravention of this Act

readings.description: Satisfaction is assessed on a two-part test: factors going to the dog (breed, training since the incident, current risk, subsequent incidents) AND factors going to the person liable for its control (insight into the causes of the earlier behaviour, compliance history, cooperation with authorities) — a dog can be behaviourally rehabilitated and the application still fail on the owner limb.

citations.cite: Hunter v City of Joondalup [2025] WASAT 36, as reported in external-modifications.json entry EM-CASELAW-33H

readings.description: Satisfaction turns solely on the dog's own current behaviour and risk profile, without regard to the owner's insight or compliance history.
readings.rejection_rationale: Reported Tribunal practice (EM-CASELAW-33H) expressly weighs the owner's capacity to control and manage the dog as part of the same satisfaction test, not as a separate consideration; a dog-only reading would ignore that guidance.

taken.rationale: The statute supplies no test of its own beyond 'satisfied' and 'likelihood of any contravention'; it is encoded as a single fact-supplied boolean carrying whatever determination the local government or Tribunal reaches, with an @ref pointing a reader to the reported two-part factor structure rather than the encoding computing it.

source.quote: The registration fee payable in relation to a dog that is bona fide used in the droving or tending of stock shall be one quarter of the fee that would otherwise be payable. ... The registration fee payable in relation to a dog's first registration ... is one half of the fee that would otherwise be payable.

readings.description: Each subsection is a pure function of an 'otherwise payable' fee supplied independently by the caller; the encoding does not itself compose s 15(5) and s 15(6) when both apply to the same dog, leaving any stacking question to whichever rule invokes both.
The discounts stack multiplicatively in a fixed order (e.g. quarter the base fee, then halve the result, or vice versa) to produce a single combined discount when both conditions are met.

taken.rationale: The statute gives each reduction as a separate, self-contained rule ('the fee that would otherwise be payable') and never addresses the case where both apply to the same dog on the same registration. Picking a stacking order and multiplier would assert a computation the text does not state; leaving each function pure and letting the caller decide is the honest encoding.

source.quote: 21. Microchipping of dogs other than dangerous dogs ... (1) ... the owner of a dog must ensure that the dog is microchipped if— ... (2) ... the owner of a dog that has reached 3 months of age must ensure that the dog is microchipped. [...] 22(6) Nothing in subsection (3) affects the operation of section 21(1) or (2) in relation to a particular dog.

citations.cite: Dog Act 1976 (WA) s 21(1)-(2), corroborated at s 22(6)

readings.description: The operative words control over the heading: s 21(1)-(2) is not textually limited to non-dangerous dogs, so it applies to every dog (dangerous or not), running concurrently with s 22's dangerous-dog-specific duty (higher penalty, its own exemption/grace-period mechanics).

citations.cite: Dog Act 1976 (WA) s 21(1)-(2), corroborated at s 22(6)

readings.description: The section heading ('Microchipping of dogs other than dangerous dogs') substantively confines s 21 to non-dangerous dogs; a dangerous dog is governed exclusively by s 22, and s 22(6) is a merely precautionary clarification.

citations.cite: Dog Act 1976 (WA) s 21(1)-(2), corroborated at s 22(6)

taken.rationale: Reading A is corroborated by s 22(6) itself, which presupposes s 21(1)/(2) keeps operating for a dog within s 22(3)'s grace-period scope -- a presupposition reading B would make s 22(6) redundant/vacuous. Further corroborated by ss 16(3)(da) and 17A(2)(d) (both outside this chunk, at lines 566 and 600 of the source), which list 'required under section 21 or 22' as two independent, non-displacing bases for registration refusal. No dog-type gate was therefore added to the s 21 offence predicates; s 22's dog-type gate is separate and additional, not a substitute.

readings.description: The offence is confined to the same actor class named in the chapeau ('the owner or occupier of that land or a person acting under his authority') whose poison-laying falls outside the lawful conditions.

source.quote: the person must keep the record ... until — (i) in relation to a dog kept for the purposes of the relevant pet shop business — the end of the period of 5 years after the day on which the relevant dog ceased being kept for the purposes of the relevant pet shop business; and (ii) in relation to a dog that is supplied or offered for supply in the course of the relevant pet shop business — the end of the period of 5 years after the day on which the dog is supplied or first offered for supply.

readings.description: s 38K(1) defines "relevant dog" disjunctively (a single dog can satisfy both limb (a) and limb (b), e.g. kept for the business then later supplied). Where both limbs apply to the same dog, the retention deadline is the LATER of the two five-year windows -- the record must be kept until BOTH applicable sub-periods (where applicable) have run.

Only whichever s 38K(1) limb currently/most-recently characterises the dog governs the retention deadline, so a later characterisation (e.g. the dog being supplied after a period of being kept) could reset or shorten an already-running retention clock.

taken.rationale: s 38K(1) states 'relevant dog ... means each of the following', an inclusive list, not mutually exclusive categories, and s 38K(3)(b) joins its two sub-limbs with 'and', not 'or'. The natural reading of a single retention duty stated in two 'and'-joined sub-limbs, applied to a subject that can independently satisfy both limbs, is that both sub-periods must be observed; letting a later characterisation shorten an already-accrued retention obligation would let the person opt into a shorter clock by their own later conduct (e.g. by finally supplying a long-kept dog), which reads oddly as a matter of statutory purpose (the record-keeping duty exists to trace a dog's provenance, which does not become less important once the dog is supplied).

taken.rationale: Materialised as the Interpretation record's `s 47(1) qualifier scope` field with both readings computed. source.quote: As soon as practicable after a local government makes a decision to grant or refuse to grant an approval to breed or a pet shop approval, or to renew or refuse to renew a pet shop approval, the local government is to enter the decision and the prescribed information in the centralised registration system.

entries.delegated_field: the S54B record's boolean field for whether entry into the centralised registration system occurred as soon as practicable (dog-act-part10-miscellaneous.l4, s 54B(1))

readings.description: Delegate satisfaction of 'as soon as practicable' to fact-supply as a single BOOLEAN field, since the Act states no day-count to derive a WITHIN deadline or day-count predicate from.
Invent a specific numeric benchmark (e.g. treat it as equivalent to the neighbouring 7-day duties in ss 54C/54E(2)) that the text does not actually state.
readings.rejection_rationale: Not adopted. The Act gives explicit numeric deadlines elsewhere in this same Part (7 days in ss 54C and 54E(2); 28/42/77/35 days in ss 54F/54H) but deliberately uses the open-textured 'as soon as practicable' standard here instead, so importing a numeric deadline from a neighbouring section would misstate the law. Delegating satisfaction of the standard to fact-supply, as a single BOOLEAN field on the S54B Record, is the honest encoding -- the same move this corpus already uses for the undefined 'satisfied' standard in s 33H (F-33H-SATISFACTION-STANDARD in dog-act-1976.l4).

source.quote: Section 38N does not apply to a person before the application day.

readings.description: "the person" in (3) refers back to the same class of person as (2)'s chapeau -- a person who conducts a relevant pet shop business immediately before the s 32 commencement day -- so (3) is one more limb of the same transitional exemption scheme, scoped to that class.
"a person" in (3) is read literally and unconditionally, granting the s 38N exemption to any person whatsoever before the application day, with no link to (2)'s pet-shop-business antecedent.
readings.rejection_rationale: Not adopted. A section titled "Transition period for relevant pet shop businesses" granting an unconditional exemption from s 38N to any person in Western Australia regardless of whether they operate such a business would be an absurd reading given the section's stated subject matter; (1)-(3) read together as one coherent transitional scheme for that one class of person.

taken.rationale: A section titled "Transition period for relevant pet shop businesses" granting an unconditional exemption from s 38N to any person in Western Australia regardless of whether they operate such a business would be an absurd reading given the section's stated subject matter; (1)-(3) read together as one coherent transitional scheme for that one class of person.
